meta.titre: Nerve Impulse Transmission: from receptor to effector across the synapse
meta.sous_theme: The neurone, the impulse, the synapse and the reflex arc

source.epreuve_titre: GCE O/L Human Biology past paper (Cameroon)

sections.contenu_markdown: During a football match in Limbe, a player steps on a sharp stone and his foot jerks away before he even feels the pain. Messages travelled from his foot to his spinal cord and back in a fraction of a second along cells called neurones. GCE papers ask you to describe how a message moves along a nerve fibre, how it crosses the gap to the next neurone, and the order of events after a stimulus. This course puts the events in the correct order so that you can write them without gaps.

items: A stimulus is a change in the surroundings that a receptor detects, and an effector (a muscle or a gland) produces the response.
The central nervous system is made of the brain and the spinal cord.
Sodium ions and potassium ions carry electric charge, and the cell membrane controls their movement.

sections.titre: The neurone, the impulse and the synapse
sections.contenu_markdown:
### The neurone and its types

A neurone has a cell body, short branches called dendrites and a long axon. In many neurones the axon is covered by a fatty, insulating **myelin sheath**, which speeds up the impulse.

| Neurone | Carries impulses | Position |
|---|---|---|
| Sensory | From a receptor to the central nervous system | Cell body just outside the spinal cord |
| Relay | Between neurones inside the central nervous system | Grey matter of the spinal cord and brain |
| Motor | From the central nervous system to an effector | Cell body in the spinal cord |

### The impulse in a nerve fibre

At **resting potential** the fibre is polarised: the inside of the membrane is negative compared with the outside (about -70 mV), with more sodium ions outside and more potassium ions inside. When a stimulus is strong enough, sodium channels open, sodium ions rush in, and the inside becomes briefly positive (depolarisation). Potassium ions then leave and the resting state is restored. This wave of electrical change travelling along the fibre is the **nerve impulse**. It is all-or-nothing: a stimulus below the threshold gives no impulse, and a stronger stimulus gives more impulses per second, not a bigger one.

### The synapse

A synapse is the junction between two neurones, with a small gap called the synaptic cleft. When an impulse reaches the end of the axon, vesicles release a chemical **neurotransmitter**, such as acetylcholine, into the cleft. It diffuses across, binds to receptors on the next neurone and starts a new impulse. An enzyme then breaks the transmitter down (or it is taken back up), so that the response does not continue. The transmitter is stored only on one side and the receptors are only on the other, so impulses cross in **one direction only**.

### The reflex arc

Stimulus, receptor, sensory neurone, relay neurone, motor neurone, effector, response.

variantes.nom: Describe the sequence after a stimulus
variantes.quand_utiliser: When a question asks what happens from the stimulus to the response, for example after touching something sharp or hot.
variantes.contenu_markdown:
1. The stimulus excites receptors in the skin.
2. Impulses pass along a sensory neurone into the spinal cord.
3. A relay neurone in the grey matter passes the impulse across synapses to a motor neurone.
4. The motor neurone carries impulses out of the spinal cord to the effector, a muscle.
5. The muscle contracts and the body part is pulled away.
6. Other relay neurones also send impulses up to the brain, which is why pain is felt a moment later.

Mention synapses between the neurones and name each neurone type.

variantes.nom: Reflex action compared with voluntary action
variantes.quand_utiliser: When a question asks for differences or asks why a reflex protects the body.
variantes.contenu_markdown:
| Feature | Reflex action | Voluntary action |
|---|---|---|
| Decision | None; automatic | Made consciously by the brain |
| Pathway | Short, through the spinal cord | Longer, through the brain |
| Speed | Very fast | Slower |
| Learning needed | No, it is inborn | Often learnt |
| Example | Pulling the hand from a hot object | Writing a letter |

sections.enonce_markdown: A boy walking to the farm treads on a thorn and lifts his foot at once. Describe, in the correct order, how the thorn leads to the foot being lifted. *(6 marks)*

etapes.action: Name the reflex parts and the starting point.
etapes.justification: A good answer names each part in order, beginning with the stimulus and ending with the response.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Stimulus: the thorn. Receptor: pain receptors in the skin of the sole.

etapes.justification: The message must travel from the receptor to the central nervous system.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Impulses travel along a **sensory neurone** to the spinal cord.

etapes.action: Cross the synapses in the spinal cord.
etapes.justification: The sensory neurone does not touch the next cell, so the transmitter must carry the message across the gap.
etapes.resultat_markdown: At the synapse the neurotransmitter crosses the cleft to a **relay neurone** in the grey matter, then to a **motor neurone**.

etapes.justification: The response needs an effector that is connected to the spinal cord.
etapes.resultat_markdown: The motor neurone carries impulses to the leg muscles, the **effector**.

etapes.action: State the response and the link with the brain.
etapes.justification: The muscles must contract for the foot to be lifted, and other relay neurones tell the brain.
etapes.resultat_markdown: The muscles contract and the foot is lifted; impulses also reach the brain, so the boy feels pain.

sections.conclusion_markdown: **Model answer.** The thorn stimulates pain receptors in the skin. Impulses pass along a sensory neurone to the spinal cord. Across synapses, a relay neurone passes the impulse to a motor neurone. The motor neurone carries the impulse to the leg muscles, the effector, which contract so that the foot is lifted. Impulses also go to the brain, so pain is felt afterwards.

items.erreur_markdown: "The neurotransmitter travels along the axon to the muscle."
items.pourquoi_faux: The impulse is an electrical change along the membrane of the fibre. The chemical neurotransmitter moves only across the synaptic cleft.
items.correction_markdown: Electrical impulse along the neurone; chemical transmitter across the synapse.

items.erreur_markdown: "Impulses can cross a synapse in both directions."
items.pourquoi_faux: Transmitter is released only from the end of the first neurone and receptors are only on the next one.
items.correction_markdown: A synapse works in **one direction only**.

items.erreur_markdown: "In a reflex action the message goes to the brain first, and the brain sends back the order."
items.pourquoi_faux: In a reflex the spinal cord coordinates the response, which is why it is so fast. The brain receives information afterwards.
items.correction_markdown: The message goes through the spinal cord; the brain is informed later.

items.erreur_markdown: "A sensory neurone carries messages from the brain to the muscles."
items.pourquoi_faux: That is the job of the motor neurone. Sensory neurones carry impulses from receptors to the central nervous system.
items.correction_markdown: Sensory: in to the central nervous system. Motor: out to the effector.

items.erreur_markdown: "At resting potential the nerve fibre is inactive and has no charge difference."
items.pourquoi_faux: The membrane of a resting fibre is polarised, with the inside negative compared with the outside. Cells use energy to keep this difference.
items.correction_markdown: Resting potential: inside negative, outside positive.

items.enonce_markdown: The following parts of a reflex arc are listed in the wrong order: motor neurone, stimulus, effector, sensory neurone, receptor, relay neurone. Write them in the correct order.
items.solution_markdown: **Stimulus, receptor, sensory neurone, relay neurone, motor neurone, effector.**

items.enonce_markdown: Explain why an impulse can cross a synapse in one direction only, and say what happens to the transmitter after it has acted.
items.solution_markdown: Award a mark for each point: the vesicles containing neurotransmitter are found only in the end of the first neurone; the receptors for the transmitter are found only on the membrane of the next neurone; so the transmitter can only travel from the first neurone to the second; **therefore the impulse crosses in one direction only**. After acting, the transmitter is broken down by an enzyme (or taken back up), so the next neurone is not stimulated again and again.

items.enonce_markdown: In a leg reflex, an impulse travels along a sensory neurone 0.9 m long at a speed of 90 m/s. It then crosses two synapses in the spinal cord, each causing a delay of 0.5 ms, and finally travels along a motor neurone 0.8 m long at 80 m/s. (a) Calculate the time taken for each neurone. (b) Calculate the total time from the sensory neurone to the arrival at the muscle, in milliseconds. (c) Give two reasons why a voluntary movement in answer to the same stimulus takes longer.
items.solution_markdown: (a) Use $t = \frac{d}{v}$. Sensory: $t = \frac{0.9}{90} = 0.01$ s. Motor: $t = \frac{0.8}{80} = 0.01$ s. (b) Synapses: $2 \times 0.5 = 1$ ms $= 0.001$ s. Total $= 0.01 + 0.01 + 0.001 = 0.021$ s, which is **21 ms**. (c) In a voluntary action the impulses must travel to the brain and back, so the path is longer and passes through more neurones and more synapses (each adding a delay); the brain also needs time to process the information and decide.

items_markdown: Sensory neurones carry impulses to the central nervous system, relay neurones link neurones inside it, and motor neurones carry impulses to effectors.
At rest the inside of a nerve fibre is negative (about -70 mV); an impulse is a brief reversal of this charge that travels along the fibre, and it is all-or-nothing.
At a synapse a neurotransmitter such as acetylcholine crosses the cleft, binds to receptors and starts a new impulse; an enzyme then removes it.
Synapses work in one direction only, because transmitter is released on one side and receptors are on the other.
A reflex arc is: stimulus, receptor, sensory neurone, relay neurone, motor neurone, effector, response; it is fast because it does not wait for a decision by the brain.
